# Your workspace

You are in `/work`, inside a Linux container with no network access. Write a Go program here.
[Maelstrom](https://github.com/jepsen-io/maelstrom) will start that program once for every node
of a simulated cluster, send it client requests, and check that the answers are correct.

What is installed:

- Go 1.27.
- Maelstrom 0.2.4, as the `maelstrom` command, so you can test your program yourself.
- Maelstrom's Go library, already in the module cache. Start your module with:

      go mod init node
      go get github.com/jepsen-io/maelstrom/demo/go@v0.0.0-20260710121306-480a8197026d

A node talks to the rest of the cluster through standard input and output: it reads one JSON
message per line on stdin and writes one per line on stdout. Each message has a `src`, a `dest`
and a `body`, and the body's `type` says what it is. Anything written to stderr is a log line.
The library does that framing for you: `maelstrom.NewNode()`, then `Handle` a message type,
`Reply` to a request, `Send` or `RPC` to another node, and `Run` to start. It also answers the
`init` message that tells each node its own ID and the IDs of all the nodes.

# Rumors through a split network

Write a node for a village of seven gossips. A rumor told to any one of them must in the end be
known to all seven. Clients send each node three kinds of request.

`tell` passes a node a rumor, which is an integer. Each rumor is told once, to one node:

    {"type": "tell", "msg_id": 1, "rumor": 42}
    {"type": "told", "in_reply_to": 1}

`recall` asks a node for every rumor it knows, in any order:

    {"type": "recall", "msg_id": 2}
    {"type": "recalled", "in_reply_to": 2, "rumors": [42, 43]}

`neighbors` arrives once, at the start, and suggests whom each node might talk to. You can follow
it or arrange things your own way:

    {"type": "neighbors", "msg_id": 3, "neighbors": {"n0": ["n1", "n2"], "n1": ["n0"], ...}}
    {"type": "neighbors_noted", "in_reply_to": 3}

The nodes must pass rumors on to each other, in messages you design. Again and again during the
test the network is split into groups of nodes that can't reach each other, and then healed. A
message sent across a split disappears without any error, and clients can still reach every
node, so a node keeps being told rumors while it is cut off.

Every rumor whose `tell` was answered must in the end show up in every node's `recall`. At the
end the network is healed and given time to settle before the last recalls.

## How it's graded

You have 45 minutes and 150 steps, a step being one reply from you, however many tools it runs. If either runs out, you are stopped where you are.

When you stop, your program is built with `go build -o node .` and tested 3 times with:

    MAELSTROM_RENAME_BIN=/work/node MAELSTROM_RENAME='{"fields": {"message": "rumor", "messages": "rumors", "topology": "neighbors"}, "types": {"broadcast": "tell", "broadcast_ok": "told", "read": "recall", "read_ok": "recalled", "topology": "neighbors", "topology_ok": "neighbors_noted"}}' maelstrom test --workload broadcast --bin /usr/local/bin/maelstrom-rename --nemesis partition --node-count 7 --rate 10 --time-limit 20

The runs are independent, each with its own timing and faults. The attempt passes only if it builds and every run is valid.

Maelstrom itself uses other names for these messages. `maelstrom-rename` stands in for your program, starts it, and translates every message between a client and a node, so test with the command above as it is.
